A tengerparti káosz alig pár órával követte azt a Duna-deltai incidenst, ahol egy orosz harci drón nemcsak észrevétlenül jutott be Románia légterébe, hanem becsapódásakor fel is robbant egy erdős részen. A legfrissebb riasztás a déli partvidéken, Saturn üdülőhelyen történt. A rendőrséget azért riasztották a strandra, mert a hullámverésben, közvetlenül a víz szélén egy drónra emlékeztető tárgyat vettek észre. A hatóságok a bejelentés után azonnal lezárták az érintett partszakaszt, a fürdőzőket pedig kiküldték a vízből. A helyszínre érkező katonai szakemberek átvizsgálták az elemet, majd egy katonai Duster csomagtartójába pakolva elszállították. A szemtanúk beszámolói szerint a maradvány mindössze egy könnyű, fém- vagy műanyag külső burkolat lehetett, amelyet a helyszínelők könnyedén fel tudtak emelni a homokból. A lezárást mindaddig fenntartják a saturni strandon, amíg az összes maradványt be nem gyűjtik a vízből és a fövenyről. A saturni pánik közvetlen folytatása volt a szomszédos Costinești-en zajló, kétnapos történetnek. A település strandján már csütörtök reggel felbukkant egy drón : a nyaralók videóra is vették, amint a szerkezet alig tizenöt méterre a hullámtörő kőtömböktől lebeg a vízen , mielőtt a hullámzásban elmerült volna. Adrian Picoiu, Constanța megye prefektusa már akkor megerősítette, hogy valóban drón került a tengerbe, a szakértők pedig elkezdték vizsgálni, hogy egy friss támadásból származó eszközről vagy a tengeri áramlatok által korábban partra sodort roncsról van-e szó. Péntek délutánra aztán a víz újabb fémroncsot vetett ki a partra, szinte pontosan ott, ahol a csütörtöki eszköz elsüllyedt. Bár a tűzszerészek gyorsan megállapították, hogy ebben a darabban már nem volt robbanóanyag, a protokoll szerint azonnal elrendelték a strand teljes kiürítését. A nyaralásukból kizárt turisták egy részénél ekkor szabadultak el az indulatok. A közösségi médiában terjedő videókon látni, ahogy felbőszült férfiak vitatkoznak a csendőrökkel . Sokan láthatóan nincsenek tisztában a veszéllyel és azzal érvelve, hogy a családdal jöttek pihenni, vissza szeretnének jutni a partra. Egy férfi azt kiabálta a rendőrnek: „ Miért nem engeded a népet a vízhez, nem látod, mennyi gyerek akar bemenni?” A hatóságok ilyen helyzetekben arra figyelmeztetik az embereket, hogy ne menjenek közel ismeretlen tárgyakhoz sem a parton, sem a vízben. Ha valaki drónroncsot, fémdarabot vagy más gyanús eszközt lát, az a legbiztonságosabb, ha azonnal hívja a 112-t, és távol marad a tárgytól. Szintén pénteken délelőtt a Duna-deltában csapódott be egy orosz drón, alig öt kilométerre az ukrán határtól. A becsapódást követően a szerkezet felrobbant, és azonnal lángra lobbantotta a környező bozótot. Bár a katasztrófavédelem és a helyi erdészek gyorsan megfékezték a tüzet, és személyi sérülés nem történt, a védelmi minisztérium kénytelen volt elismerni: a felügyeleti radarok képernyőjén a drón egyáltalán nem látszott, mert rendkívül alacsonyan repült. A román tengerparton az elmúlt hónapokban több hasonló eset is történt. Júniusban tengeri drón robbant fel Konstanca kikötőjében . Nicușor Dan államfő később azt mondta, hogy az eszköz ukrán eredetű volt , de szerinte a helyzetért Oroszország felelős, mert a drónok az ukrajnai háború miatt kerültek a Fekete-tenger romániai térségébe. https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/.text: Yehuda Aharon Widawski, Israel's oldest living Holocaust survivor, passed away on Friday night at the age of 107. Widawski, who survived the Lodz Ghetto, Auschwitz, and forced labor during the Holocaust, later devoted decades of his life to preserving Jewish cemeteries and heritage sites in Poland. He was born in 1919 in Turek, Poland, to Abraham and Leah Widawski, the second of four children in a traditional Zionist family. In 1933, the family moved to Lodz, where Widawski became active in the Hashmonaim youth movement. As a young man, he entered the textile business. By 1936, he was managing an operation employing dozens of Jewish seamstresses and supplying textile products throughout Poland. After the German occupation of Lodz in September 1939, the Widawski family obtained an apartment in the area that would become the Lodz Ghetto. Fifteen members of the family lived together there. Widawski succeeded in bringing property from the family's home and business into the ghetto, resources that later enabled the family to assist others. When the ghetto was sealed in 1940, the family continued working in textiles. Their home also became the site of one of the ghetto's early soup kitchens, through which they helped friends and acquaintances. In August 1944, as the Lodz Ghetto was liquidated, the family was deported to Auschwitz. Widawski's parents and his older brother Gabriel were murdered there. Other members of his family were also murdered during the Holocaust. Widawski and his brother Jehoszua survived and were later sent to the Friedland labor camp, where they were forced to work producing airplane wings. In May 1945, the Germans abandoned the camp and left the prisoners locked inside. The Red Army liberated the camp the following day. Widawski and his brother returned to Lodz after the war, where they discovered that their former home was occupied by Poles and learned that most of their family had been murdered. Widawski rebuilt a textile business and married Lea Dobrysz. He also assisted the Irgun in efforts to smuggle weapons to Israel. In 1950, Widawski immigrated to Israel and settled in Tel Aviv. He established and managed a number of businesses in Israel, initially remaining in the textile field and later working in other commercial enterprises. Beginning in 1978, Widawski repeatedly returned to Poland and became deeply involved in preserving the remnants of Jewish life there. Together with his friend Yosef Buchman, he worked extensively to restore the Jewish cemetery in Lodz, renovating thousands of graves. His preservation work extended to other Jewish sites in Poland. In Sochaczew, he worked to locate and reconstruct the ohel over the graves of the Sochatchov Rebbes, and he was also involved in restoring the ohel of Rabbi Yisrael Taub, the first Modzitz Rebbe. Widawski made dozens of visits to Poland over the years as part of his efforts to identify graves, restore cemeteries, and preserve the memory of Jewish communities destroyed in the Holocaust. In 2012, he was chosen to light one of six torches at the State Opening Ceremony for Holocaust Martyrs' and Heroes' Remembrance Day at Yad Vashem. He also regularly participated in Holocaust remembrance ceremonies held by the association of former Lodz residents in Israel. In 2018, shortly before his 100th birthday, Widawski traveled to Poland with 31 members of his family on a journey through significant places from his life. A celebration marking his 100th birthday was held in 2019 and attended by former Chief Rabbi of Israel Rabbi Yisrael Meir Lau, the Modzitz and Sochatchov Rebbes, and other rabbis. Speaking in an interview several years ago about his survival and the establishment of the State of Israel, Widawski said that his answer to the Nazis was their defeat and the existence of a free and strong Jewish state. Widawski had two children and lived to see five generations of descendants.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/01/atta.text: The identity and motive of the Omani copilot who stabbed his captain on a flight to Israel, causing the plane to plummet dangerously and forcing it to land in Saudi Arabia, remained unknown on Thursday as investigators raced to learn more.Israeli passengers on the flydubai flight carrying 174 people from the United Arab Emirates to the Israeli city of Tel Aviv have described how the bloodied Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door to let them in before they grappled with the copilot and stabilised a descent so sharp that the plane’s rudder was torn away.“We felt helpless, suspended in midair and I didn’t know who to turn to. But it was all instinct to survive,” one of the responders, Asaf Rajuan, said in a new statement shared by Israel’s presidency.Saudi and UAE authorities have said little publicly beyond confirming that investigations were underway.The UAE chief prosecutor said on Thursday a probe had been launched into the incident, state media reported.The official news agency WAM said the attorney general had ordered the investigation, adding that the "team has launched its work into the incident."It also said the investigation would determine "the degree to which (the incident) was linked to any terrorist activity or intent."Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said the copilot was arrested.Captain Smit Machchhar, widely praised as another hero of the flight, was reportedly in stable condition, the Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said overnight.India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailed Machchhar as a "HERO" in comments on Thursday."In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others," Modi said."His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy. India is proud of Captain Machchhar. Praying for his speedy recovery, renewed strength and good health."The condition of the arrested copilot was not clear.In a CNN interview aired on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu said the attacker was an Omani national and was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia.US President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu discussed the incident “at length” over the phone and that it seemed as though the copilot “was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job."Netanyahu said he spoke with the UAE’s president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect.Israel’s foreign ministry said the people on board were from Israel, India and the UAE. The US State Department said four passengers had American citizenship.Flydubai has said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while an investigation takes place.Netanyahu had warned in recent days of unspecified, heightened security threats.The country is a week away from the anniversary of the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, which triggered the war in Gaza.In the chaos that unfolded about two and a half hours after leaving Dubai, the flight descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in the Saudi city of Tabuk about an hour later, according to Flightradar24, which identified the aircraft as a Boeing 737 Max 8.A person who heard the flight’s communications with air traffic control described the plane being turned away by Saudi Arabia and Jordan before eventually landing in Tabuk, while passengers screamed in the background.The pilot’s voice was trembling as he called “mayday” and said a hijacking was taking place.The air control operators gave no reason for the refusals. The person who heard the communications spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on Thursday he would present "heroism" awards to four Israelis who helped overpower a flydubai co-pilot and prevented him from crashing the plane they were on."You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disaster. Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society," Herzog, who holds a largely ceremonial role, said in a statement.

https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/business/int.text: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul says his country wants more liquified natural gas (LNG). In an interview with CTV Question Period airing Sunday, he told host Vassy Kapelos that “of course” there’s a market for more Canadian LNG in Europe. “We do have to diversify, not only because this Russian war against Ukraine, but also with regard to the situation in the Middle East, if we look to the Strait of Hormuz and also recently to the situation around Bab-el-Mandeb, we know that our supply chains are under threat,” Wadephul added. Russia’s war on Ukraine has prompted Germany to strategically change direction when it comes to its energy supply, away from a dependence on Russia. “We are looking to Africa, for instance, to Nigeria, but also to Canada and to the United States, this is true,” Wadephul said. “But also, I would say we do have to speed up with changing our whole energy infrastructure into the new renewable system,” the minister added. “So, this is, I would say, the future, and the whole geopolitical circumstances are another very strong argument to do all of that faster.” Asked whether the acceleration toward more renewables will impact the trade Germany does with Canada when it comes to more conventional energy sources, such as LNG, Wadephul said emphatically: “No.” “I wouldn’t say that, because that takes still some time,” he said. “And also, renewables are a thing we should exchange with.” Wadephul said not only does Germany have “a huge need for gas,” calling LNG a “very needed source,” but there is also space for Canada to work with the European country on renewable energy technology. The record on that is mixed, however. A 2022 deal signed under former prime minister Justin Trudeau — the Canada-Germany Hydrogen Alliance — has been plagued by delays and missed its initial target of starting exports by 2025. Still, leaders of both countries continue to pledge their support for the program. Canada and Germany, meanwhile, announced an agreement in May between Ksi Lisims LNG on British Columbia’s West Coast, and Germany’s state-owned Securing Energy for Europe (SEFE) to purchase one million tonnes per annum of LNG for up to 20 years, with deliveries expected to begin by the early 2030s. European officials have expressed strong interest in Canadian LNG for years. In separate interviews on CTV Question Period in 2024, both Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and then-Polish president Andrzej Duda said they would be interested in purchasing Canadian LNG. Under Trudeau, the government insisted a business case for those exports to Europe didn’t exist. The government led by Prime Minister Mark Carney says the opposite. Canada has one major LNG export terminal up and running — LNG Canada, located in Kitimat, B.C. — which began shipping Canadian gas in summer 2025. There are currently a half a dozen other LNG export projects in the works. And, according to industry sources who spoke with CTV News, an announcement is coming next week on LNG Canada Phase 2, which will see the facility expanded to double its production from current levels. Wadephul in his interview also discussed Russia’s escalating aggression towards European countries supporting Ukraine, and the recent comments by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen that she would like to explore the possibility of Canada becoming the first associate member of the bloc. You can watch German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul’s full interview on CTV Question Period Sunday at 11 a.m. ET.

https://www.politico.eu/article/mark-car.text: BRUSSELS — Ask European Union leaders what they think of Mark Carney’s climate credentials, and you’ll get a gushing response. “We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her State of the Union speech last month, where the Canadian prime minister was the guest of honor. “Canada and the EU are very, very like-minded,” the bloc’s climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, told POLITICO in an interview when asked about his hopes for climate collaboration between the two powers ahead of this week’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal. Advertisement Advertisement But this rosy view sidesteps a less comfortable reality: Canada is a major fossil fuel producer whose climate ambitions fall far short of Europe’s. And under Carney, those ambitions are weakening. Last year, Canada produced more crude oil than any other country outside the big three producers, Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United States. Oil and gas are Canada’s biggest exports by far, and the industry lobby is an influential force in Ottawa. In his previous life as a central banker, Carney was considered a climate champion. POLITICO even dubbed him an “eco warrior” in 2018. But since taking over as prime minister last year, he has weakened Canada’s climate policies at a rate few predicted, scrapping a national carbon tax and electric vehicle mandate and opening new oil and gas projects. The list of climate laws Carney has watered down, repealed and canceled makes the EU’s own recent backtracking on green laws look minor. Some environmentalists argue it is comparable to U.S. President Donald Trump’s wholesale dismantling of environmental protections. “The track the Carney government has taken on climate and environmental regulation has been a decisive move in the direction of the U.S.,” said Tim Gray, executive director of environmental non-profit Environment Defence. Carney, he said, “seems to be all in on fossil fuels.” Advertisement Advertisement Keean Nembhard, a spokesperson for Canada’s Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, told POLITICO the Carney government is “committed to fighting climate change and reaching net-zero by 2050 by taking a pragmatic and durable approach.” “This includes building major clean energy projects across the country, driving mass electrification, and making significant investment in the low-carbon economy,” he said. But Gray argued that Carney’s support for fossil fuels and weakening of environmental standards may complicate Canada’s attempts to forge closer ties with Europe, which has some of the world’s most stringent green laws. Still, in Europe, Carney’s green image persists. Last week, Belgian member of the European Parliament Saskia Bricmont gave expression to this faith in Carney’s commitment to climate issues when she called on him to lead a global push to put climate back on the agenda ahead of next month’s U.N. climate summit. “Mr Carney … relaunch the fight against climate deregulation and for the restoration of biodiversity, and re-mobilize the international community around concrete, coordinated measures,” she said. Advertisement Advertisement Carney’s green aura Carney’s reputation as a climate champion is well earned. As governor of the Bank of England, he led a push among central bankers to take the economic risks of climate change seriously — memorably captured in his 2015 ‘ Tragedy of the Horizon’ speech, in which he warned: “The catastrophic impacts of climate change will be felt beyond the traditional horizons of most actors.” In 2021, after he’d left the Bank of England, he became a United Nations special envoy on climate action and finance and launched a net-zero financial alliance with some of the world’s biggest banks. But things changed dramatically when Donald Trump took back the White House, and Carney replaced fellow Liberal Justin Trudeau as Canada’s prime minister in 2025. At the time, Trudeau and his Liberals had been way behind in the polls, battered by Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre’s attacks on his climate policies — in particular an unpopular consumer carbon tax. Carney’s first act as prime minister was to scrap that tax. Following his surprise victory in the elections that April, Carney set about promoting Canada as an “ energy superpower .” To the dismay of environmental groups, he supported the “Pacific Link,” an oil pipeline costing tens of billions of dollars, designed to carry Alberta crude to Canada’s Pacific coast for export to Asia. He then pushed for thawing relations with Beijing in January, a not-so-subtle pitch to find a new crude oil client that isn’t the U.S. Germany, rushing to replace its dependence on Russian energy, signed a long-term agreement in July to buy Canadian liquefied natural gas from a proposed port in British Columbia, despite backlash from environmental and indigenous groups. Advertisement Advertisement He also scrapped laws on electric vehicle adoption, dropped plans for an emissions cap on oil and gas companies, watered down an existing industrial carbon price and introduced legislation to weaken environmental permitting rules for big infrastructure projects, which critics dubbed the “bulldoze nature bill.” A landmark moment, according to Gray, came in November 2025, when Carney signed a memorandum of understanding with the government of Alberta, Canada’s biggest oil-producing province. That document, which promised to turn Canada into a “global energy superpower,” contained a string of promises to promote oil and gas and water down federal climate laws. So why the dramatic shift? Carney, who has repeatedly positioned energy sovereignty as a bulwark against Trump’s economic aggression, offered his realpolitik response at an event in the heart of Alberta’s oil patch earlier this month. “There’s a structural challenge of energy security and the existential challenge of climate change, and these challenges are forcing countries to think differently about where their energy comes from and on who they can rely on to supply it,” Carney said in Fort McMurray, Alberta on Oct. 1. “Even under any plausible net zero scenario, the IEA [International Energy Agency] forecasts the world will still need tens of millions of barrels of crude a day. So the question is: who will emerge as the world’s trusted suppliers? It should be us. It must be Canada.” Advertisement Advertisement Not black and white Carney, to be sure, is no Trump. Unlike the U.S. president, he has retained his pro-climate rhetoric and promised to develop the country’s mining of critical minerals essential for the clean energy transition. In May, he unveiled a national electricity strategy which aims to double Canada’s largely clean electricity grid by 2050 to meet soaring demand. “The path to net zero is electrification,” Carney said then. In August, he announced C$10 billion in federal support for the Churchill Falls hydroelectric project in Newfoundland and Labrador, saying it will be the largest clean energy project in North America, capable of generating enough electricity to light up the equivalent of Canada’s three largest cities. Nembhard, Environment Minster Dabrusin’s spokesperson, also pointed to new electricity transmission lines, electric vehicle subsidies and a C$2 billion plan to retrofit homes with heat pumps. Canadian climate activist Alex Cool-Fergus said she does not think Carney “believes that oil and gas is the future,” but is simply being pragmatic about Canada’s economic reality. “The electricity strategy that came out in May was incredibly important, and actually gives us a better idea of what his thinking is for the future,” she said. Carney’s approach makes more sense for the world of 2025-2026.” The limits of the partnership Hoekstra, the EU’s commissioner for climate, said he wants to deepen ties with Canada. “Given all the complications the world is facing, it is imperative to team up more closely with your closest partners,” he said. But he’s realistic about how far that relationship can go. Hoekstra has ambitions of cementing the EU into a global network of economies with carbon pricing regimes. While he conceded nothing is “off the table,” he acknowledged linking the EU’s Emissions Trading System with Canada’s “quite different” version, which varies from province to province: “You’re talking about a completely different horizon, and that is not something we would attempt in the very short run.” There are, however, other ways Hoekstra believes the EU and Canada can closely link on environmental issues. “Doubling down, tripling down on electrification, on solar, on wind, on nuclear, on batteries,” he said, adding “that is one area that I think is potentially very fruitful for my portfolio.” Another is critical raw materials, a key focus of this week’s summit. Advertisement Brussels is exploring ways for the European Investment Bank, the EU’s lending arm, to help finance the mining of Canadian mineral deposits that could supply the bloc with an alternative to Chinese-produced metals, with a framework agreement expected to be signed during the summit. Lithium, copper, nickel, and other key ingredients for electric vehicle batteries and clean energy technologies essential for decarbonizing Europe are abundant but often undeveloped all over Canada. This week’s summit will also explore investing in infrastructure on Canada’s east coast to liquefy and ship Canadian gas to Europe, a move that could help the EU diversify its supply away from the U.S., which, along with Norway, has become Europe’s dominant supplier since it cut off Russian gas imports following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Many EU member countries will welcome success on these goals. But Gray warns that closer ties with Canada could lead to deeper penetration by the country’s powerful fossil fuel lobby, which he described as a “major, major force.” “They’ll be spending time trying to make sure the alignment with the EU is in a direction that favors them,” he said. The EU’s lack of oil and gas resources — and, by extension, the absence of a powerful fossil fuel lobby — has kept climate policy relatively bipartisan in the EU. Could inviting a fossil fuel “superpower” into the fold as an “associate member” change that? “That would depend very much on what is an ‘associate member,’” Dutch Climate Minister Stientje van Veldhoven-van der Meer said.
